He stood up and left the room with my nurse. A moment later, my father came in.

Nothing could have made me happier just then than seeing my father. I held out my hand to him and cried,

"Are you safe, then—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?"

My father reassured me that they were all well. He tried to lift my spirits by talking about the people so dear to me, but soon realized that a prison could never be a cheerful place. "What a place you are living in, my son!" he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and the miserable room. "You set out in search of happiness, but some terrible fate seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—"

Hearing the name of my unhappy, murdered friend was more than I could bear in my weakened condition. I began to cry.

"Ah, yes, Father," I answered. "Some dreadful destiny hangs over me, and I must live to carry it out. Otherwise, surely I would have died beside Henry's coffin."

We could not talk for long. My health was still so uncertain that every care had to be taken to keep me calm. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that I must not wear myself out. But my father's presence seemed like that of a guardian angel to me, and little by little my health returned.

As the illness left me, a deep and terrible sadness took hold, and nothing could drive it away. I constantly saw Clerval before me, murdered and ghastly. More than once these thoughts upset me so greatly that my friends feared I would become dangerously ill again. Why had they kept such a miserable, hated creature alive? Surely only so that I could fulfil the destiny that is now nearing its end. Soon, very soon, death will still my beating heart and free me from the enormous weight of suffering that crushes me. In carrying out the sentence of justice, I too shall find rest. Back then death seemed far away, though I thought constantly of wishing to die. I would often sit for hours without moving or speaking, hoping for some great upheaval that would bury both me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The time for the court sessions drew near. I had already spent three months in prison. Though still weak and always at risk of falling ill again, I had to travel almost a hundred miles to the county town where the court met. Mr. Kirwin took full responsibility for gathering witnesses and preparing my defence.

These were the finest times and the most terrible times, an age of wisdom and an age of folly, an era of faith and an era of disbelief, a season of Light and a season of Darkness, a springtime of hope and a winter of despair. Everything lay ahead of us; nothing lay ahead of us. We were all heading straight to Heaven; we were all heading straight in the opposite direction. In short, the period so closely resembled our own that some of its loudest authorities demanded it be described, whether favorably or unfavorably, only in the strongest possible terms.

A king with a large jaw and a plain-faced queen occupied England's throne; a king with a large jaw and a beautiful queen occupied France's. In both countries, the guardians of the State's exclusive stores of wealth and patronage considered it perfectly obvious that the existing order would last forever.

The year was seventeen seventy-five. England was granted spiritual revelations in that privileged age, just as it is today. Mrs. Southcott had recently celebrated her blessed twenty-fifth birthday. A prophetic private in the Life Guards had foretold her glorious arrival by announcing that preparations were complete for London and Westminster to be swallowed up. Only twelve years had passed since the Cock-lane ghost was finally laid to rest, after tapping out its messages as the spirits of this very last year, supernaturally lacking in imagination, tapped out theirs. More ordinary messages concerning earthly affairs had recently reached the English Crown and people from a congress of British subjects in America. Strange as it may sound, these have turned out to matter more to humanity than anything yet communicated through any offspring of the Cock-lane brood.

France, generally less blessed in spiritual matters than her sister with the shield and trident, glided downhill with extraordinary ease, printing paper money and spending it. Guided by her Christian pastors, she also amused herself with such humane accomplishments as condemning a young man to have his hands severed, his tongue pulled out with pincers, and his body burned alive. His offense was failing to kneel in the rain to honor a filthy procession of monks that had passed within his sight, some fifty or sixty yards away. It is quite likely that, when this sufferer was executed, trees stood growing in the forests of France and Norway that the Woodman, Fate, had already marked for felling. Their timber would be sawn into boards to construct a certain movable frame, equipped with a sack and a knife, that would become terrible in history.

"Well now, Mr. Bumble," he said at last, "one cannot deny that since the new feeding arrangements were introduced, the coffins have grown rather narrower and shallower than formerly; but we must earn something, Mr. Bumble. Properly seasoned wood is a costly commodity, sir; and every iron handle travels here by canal from Birmingham."

"Well, well," answered Mr. Bumble, "there are disadvantages in every calling. A reasonable profit is certainly permitted."

"Certainly, certainly," returned the undertaker; "and when I make nothing on one article or another, I recover it over the longer run, you understand—he! he! he!"

"Precisely," said Mr. Bumble.

"Although I must observe," the undertaker went on, returning to the train of remarks interrupted by the beadle, "I must observe, Mr. Bumble, that there is one tremendous difficulty I have to struggle with: the stout people are always the quickest to go. Those who enjoyed better circumstances and paid their rates for years are the first to succumb upon entering the house; and I assure you, Mr. Bumble, three or four inches beyond one's estimate eats seriously into one's earnings, particularly with a family to support, sir."

Mr. Sowerberry delivered this with the proper indignation of a man unfairly treated; and Mr. Bumble, feeling that it cast something of a slur upon the parish's honour, judged it prudent to introduce another subject. Oliver Twist was foremost in his thoughts, so Oliver became his topic.

"By the way," said Mr. Bumble, "you wouldn't happen to know anyone needing a boy? A porochial apprentice, at present a dead weight—a millstone, I might call him, about the porochial neck? Generous terms, Mr. Sowerberry, generous terms?" Speaking thus, Mr. Bumble lifted his cane towards the notice overhead and struck three separate taps upon the words "five pounds," displayed there in enormous Roman capitals.

"Gadso!" exclaimed the undertaker, catching hold of the gold-trimmed lapel of Mr. Bumble's official coat. "That is exactly what I meant to discuss with you. You see—dear me, what an exceedingly handsome button, Mr. Bumble! I had never remarked it before."

"Yes, I find it quite attractive," said the beadle, looking down proudly at the great brass buttons adorning his coat. "The design matches the porochial seal—the Good Samaritan tending the sick and battered man. The board gave it to me on New Year's morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember first putting it on to go to the inquest upon that impoverished tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight."
